body_text:
Six Winters, Somebody Plowed Her Driveway Before Dawn and Never Said a Word. When She Finally Caught Him, He Explained It in Nine.

Picture a gravel road in a county where the snow means it.

Picture a woman at the end of it, at five in the morning, standing at her window with a coffee, looking at a driveway that has already been cleared.

Call her Corinne.

And picture the truck two properties down with its lights still on and a blade on the front, pulling back onto the road. Call the man in it Herb.

This has happened every storm for six years. Corinne has never asked him to. She has never successfully thanked him.

And the morning she finally catches him, he's going to explain the whole thing in nine words, and those nine words are going to reorganize her kitchen.

Let me back up. You need Corinne first, and you have met her.

Corinne is fifty-eight, and for nineteen years she has driven a school bus.

Which means her day is not a day. It's three pieces of a day with holes cut between them.

She's on the road at five-forty. Route by six-fifteen. Done by eight-thirty, home by nine.

Then the hole: the middle of the day, which sounds like freedom and functions like a waiting room, because the afternoon route starts at two-fifteen and everything in her life has to fit around the fact that a bus is going to need her at two-fifteen.

Home again by four-thirty. Some nights, an activity run to a ball game two towns over, back at ten.

Nineteen years of that. She's good at it — the kids' names, the parents' cars, the one hill that's a problem in February.

And here's the thing about Corinne that makes her story worth telling, because it is emphatically not a story about a woman who doesn't try.

Corinne does everything right.

Look at what she owns.

There's a stationary bike in the spare room, bought after real research, the good one that people say lasts.

There's a sewing machine — her mother's, rebuilt at a shop two counties over, because Corinne wanted it done properly.

There's a bread machine. A stock pot heavy enough to be a family heirloom. A set of good walking boots, broken in, waiting by the closet door.

And there's the shelf. Everyone has the shelf. Hers holds the tea with the good intentions, the two canisters, the vitamin sampler her sister sent, all bought carefully, all tried twice.

Nothing on that list is a mistake. Every single item was chosen by a competent adult who read about it first.

That's what makes the next part strange, and it's the thing Corinne has never once been able to explain to herself.

None of it runs.

Not from lack of wanting. Not from lack of trying — she starts things constantly, and she starts them well, which is somehow worse.

She'd tell you, if you asked her at a church supper and she'd had a glass of wine, that she does everything right and it doesn't take. That she has the equipment of a person with a good life and the calendar of a person who's waiting for one.

It isn't a crisis. It's a hum — a low, standing puzzlement about why a woman this prepared has so few things that actually happen.

She has decided, privately, that it's a discipline problem, because that's what everyone decides.

She's wrong, and it's going to take a man with a plow to prove it.

So: the snow.

Corinne's road is gravel and the county gets to it when it gets to it. Everyone out there handles their own driveway.

And for six winters, hers has handled itself.

The first time, she assumed a mistake — somebody with a contract and a wrong address. The second time she watched the tracks and figured out the direction they came from.

By the fourth or fifth storm she knew it was Herb, who is somewhere in his seventies, who used to run a road grader for the county for thirty-one years, and who plows the driveways of most of the road before the sun comes up.

Not for money. There's no arrangement. There's no note. There has never been a conversation about it.

Corinne has tried to thank him three times. Once with a check, which came back in her mailbox torn in half — not unkindly, just decisively. Once with a plate at Christmas, which was accepted with a nod and never discussed. Once by flagging him down on the road, which produced a wave and a truck that kept moving.

So it stands: it snows, she wakes up, the driveway is clear, and the world contains one thing she didn't have to solve.

Then comes the morning in February, and this is where the story turns.

Big storm overnight, and Corinne is up earlier than usual because a storm means the district's phone tree and the phone tree means she's awake at four-thirty regardless.

Which is how she comes to be standing at the end of her own driveway with a coffee in each hand when Herb's truck comes up out of the dark.

He can't really pretend not to see a woman standing in her own driveway holding two coffees at four-forty in the morning.

He rolls the window down.

She hands one up. He takes it, because refusing a coffee in that weather would be theater and neither of them has time.

And Corinne — nineteen years of talking to sleepy teenagers has made her extremely good at asking direct questions without heat — says the thing she's been saving for six winters.

"How do you do this? Not why. How. You do half the road. Every storm. Before dawn."

Herb looks at her for a second. Then he looks at his blade, and then back at her, and gives the answer.

"Plow's been on since the first week of November."

That's it. That's the nine words.

Corinne waits for more, the way you do.

And Herb, who is not a philosopher and would be offended by the suggestion, elaborates only because the coffee is hot and he's holding it.

"It goes on in November. Comes off in April. In between, I don't do anything. I get in the truck."

He nods down the road, at the dark shapes of the other places.

"Fellas out here have plows. Good ones. Better'n mine, some of 'em. And they take 'em off in between — makes sense, right? Rig's heavy, it's hard on the front end, hard to park. Sensible. So it comes off after every storm."

He drinks some of the coffee.

"First storm, they all plow. Second storm, most of 'em plow. By the third one, half those trucks are sitting there with the plow leaning against the garage wall, and everybody's shoveling."

And then the sentence Corinne is going to think about on the whole morning route, and at two-fifteen, and for a good long while after:

"Nobody ever quits the plowing, ma'am. They quit the mounting. Twenty minutes in the cold with a wrench before you can even start — that's what beats a man. Not the snow."

He hands the cup back, mostly empty.

"I just never take it off. That's the whole trick. Ain't a discipline thing. I'm the laziest man on this road."

Then he puts the truck in gear and goes and does two more driveways before it's properly light.

Corinne drives her route that morning with the heater cycling and the kids not talking because it's early, and she does the arithmetic.

You knew she would. So did she, somewhere around the second stop.

Because she is not thinking about snow. She's thinking about the spare room, and the sewing machine, and the good stock pot, and the boots by the door.

She's thinking about every single thing she owns that requires mounting the plow.

Start with the bike. The bike is in the spare room, and the spare room is also where the laundry lands, so the bike needs twenty minutes of clearing before it needs twenty minutes of riding. Setup: twenty. Teardown: some.

The sewing machine lives in its case under the stairs. To sew, she has to haul it up, clear the dining table, find the box with the thread, set the light. An hour before a stitch. And afterward, all of it in reverse, because the table is where they eat.

The stock pot means the big cutting board, the two knives, the produce washed and prepped, and then the pot itself, which does not fit in the dishwasher and never will.

The bread machine — the bread machine is honest work, but it's a flour canister, a wiped counter, an ingredients hunt, and a bucket to wash by hand.

Even the boots. The good broken-in boots by the door require a jacket, a hat, gloves, the dog's leash if she takes him, and a reckoning with the fact that the good walking road is eleven minutes away by car.

Every single item on Corinne's list of good intentions has a plow that has to be mounted before it can do anything at all.

And her day — the three-pieces day, with a bus at two-fifteen and a phone tree at four-thirty — has almost no window anywhere in it that's big enough for mounting.

That's it. That's the whole thing.

For years she has believed she was a woman who couldn't stick with anything. What she actually is, and has always been, is a woman whose day cannot accommodate setup.

The tasks were never the problem. She has energy for the tasks. She likes the tasks.

What she doesn't have is twenty minutes in the cold with a wrench, over and over, forever, before anything begins.

And here's the cruelty of it, the part that took a man with a blade to make visible:

Nobody sees setup. Setup doesn't look like anything. It has no name in anybody's calendar, and it never shows up in the story people tell about themselves.

So when the bike doesn't get ridden, the story is "I don't have the discipline." Never "the room is full and the clearing is the tax."

When the sewing machine stays under the stairs, the story is "I let that go." Never "the mounting costs an hour and my day is in three pieces."

Corinne has been paying a tax she couldn't see and then blaming her character for the bill.

That's the discovery, and it's worth saying plainly:

People almost never quit the thing. They quit the setup. And when the setup is expensive enough, quitting looks exactly like a character flaw, from the inside as well as the outside.

The fix isn't more willpower. Herb is, by his own cheerful testimony, the laziest man on the road.

The fix is picking the version of the thing that's already mounted — the one with nothing between you and it.

Which brings this story — through that door, and no other — to beets.

Picture a woman at the end of it, at five in the morning, standing at her window with a coffee, looking at a driveway that has already been cleared.

Call her Corinne.

This has happened every storm for six years. Corinne has never asked him to. She has never successfully thanked him.

Let me back up. You need Corinne first, and you have met her.

Corinne is fifty-eight, and for nineteen years she has driven a school bus.

She's on the road at five-forty. Route by six-fifteen. Done by eight-thirty, home by nine.

Then the hole: the middle of the day, which sounds like freedom and functions like a waiting room, because the afternoon route starts at two-fifteen and everything in her life has to fit around the fact that a bus is going to need her at two-fifteen.

Nineteen years of that. She's good at it — the kids' names, the parents' cars, the one hill that's a problem in February.

Corinne does everything right.

Look at what she owns.

There's a stationary bike in the spare room, bought after real research, the good one that people say lasts.

There's a sewing machine — her mother's, rebuilt at a shop two counties over, because Corinne wanted it done properly.

None of it runs.

She has decided, privately, that it's a discipline problem, because that's what everyone decides.

She's wrong, and it's going to take a man with a plow to prove it.

cards.body:
Around half of people are worried they’ll lose their job to AI. 

They’re right to be concerned: AI can now complete real-world coding tasks on GitHub, generate photorealistic video, drive a taxi more safely than humans, and do accurate medical diagnosis. And it’s set to continue to improve rapidly.

But what’s less appreciated is that, while AI drives down the value of skills it can do, it drives up the value of skills it can’t — because they become the bottlenecks to further automation (for a while at least). 

Your best strategy is to learn the skills that AI will make more valuable, trying to ride the wave one step ahead of automation. 

Read more about what economic theory and recent data can tell us about the uncertain future for different fields of work, and how you could plan to adapt to it:
cards.title: How not to lose your job to AI
cards.link_description: While AI drives down the value of skills it can do, it drives up the value of skills it can’t
cards.caption: 80000hours.org

cards.body:
Half of people are worried about losing their job to AI, and that's a fair concern given how capabilities are growing.

However, while AI drives down the value of skills it can do, it drives up the value of everything else it can't.

So, what skills are those?
cards.title: The skills AI will make more valuable (and how to learn them)
cards.link_description: What economic theory and recent data tells us about the next stage of AI automation
cards.caption: 80000hours.org

cards.body:
Which skills will be hardest to automate, as AI continues to progress? 

1. Tasks not in AI training data

Many skills that are difficult for humans to learn, including much of therapy, medical diagnosis, and coding, can be done pretty well by ‘pattern matching’ systems.

However, LLMs remain bad at a lot of things, typically including tasks missing from their training data. 

For example, controlling robotics. While the internet contains a huge amount of linguistic data, there’s no equivalent store of data describing physical movement, and it's not trivial to create it. 

2. Messy, long-horizon skills

New-generation AI systems have made dramatic progress in domains where answers can be immediately verified, like maths and coding, making them very suitable for reinforcement learning. 

In contrast, consider a skill like building a company: many judgement calls, with no obviously correct answers, no massive datasets on the individual steps, and success only determined over years.

3. Skills where a person-in-the-loop is wanted

Even if AI can technically do a task, it might not be allowed to do so where people still want a person-in-the-loop — for legal liability, to sense-check for hallucinations, or to retain the 'human touch' in art or childcare, for example. 

4. Skills where automation is bottlenecked by physical infrastructure

Relatively slow robot production and the lack of data about physical tasks will create a period where their automation lags behind cognitive tasks.

Even AI’s deployment to cognitive tasks will be somewhat bottlenecked by available computing power, especially if early systems use a lot of test-time compute. 


Read more about the skills most likely to increase in value, and to get started on learning them:

cards.title: How not to lose your job to AI

cards.body:
Around half of people are worried they’ll lose their job to AI. 

They’re right to be concerned: AI can now complete real-world coding tasks on GitHub, generate photorealistic video, drive a taxi more safely than humans, and do accurate medical diagnosis. And it’s set to continue to improve rapidly.

But what’s less appreciated is that, while AI drives down the value of skills it can do, it drives up the value of skills it can’t — because they become the bottlenecks to further automation (for a while at least).

body_text:
n the tapestry of human history, few technological advancements have promised to alter the fabric of society as profoundly as Artificial Intelligence (AI). Once a fixture of science fiction novels and cinematic imagination, AI has rapidly transitioned into an omnipresent reality, subtly yet deeply embedding itself into our daily routines, global industries, and cognitive frameworks. From the algorithms that curate our social media feeds to autonomous vehicles navigating complex urban landscapes, we are living in an era defined by intelligent machines. This technological revolution offers unprecedented opportunities to solve some of humanity’s most complex challenges, but it also forces us to confront deep ethical dilemmas and existential questions about what it means to be human.
At the forefront of the AI revolution is its remarkable potential to enhance human capability and productivity. In the field of healthcare, machine learning algorithms are analyzing vast datasets of medical imaging and genetic sequences with a speed and accuracy that surpass human capabilities. This has led to the early detection of life-threatening diseases like cancer and the rapid development of novel pharmaceuticals, effectively saving countless lives. Similarly, in environmental science, AI systems are being deployed to model climate change patterns, optimize renewable energy grids, and track deforestation in real-time. By processing variables too complex for the human mind to grasp simultaneously, AI acts as a cognitive amplifier, enabling scientists and policymakers to make data-driven decisions to protect our planet.
Furthermore, AI is fundamentally restructuring the global economy and the nature of work. Automation and intelligent systems have streamlined manufacturing pipelines, optimized supply chains, and revolutionized customer service through sophisticated natural language processing. While critics traditionally feared that automation would lead to widespread unemployment, historical trends suggest a more nuanced reality: a shift in the labor paradigm. While routine, repetitive tasks are increasingly handled by machines, new industries are emerging, creating a high demand for roles centered around AI ethics, data engineering, and human-machine collaboration. The workplace of the future will likely not be one where humans are replaced by AI, but rather one where humans who use AI replace those who do not.
However, this rapid integration of technology is not without its dark side. The rise of AI brings forth pressing ethical concerns, chief among them being algorithmic bias and the erosion of privacy. Because AI systems learn from historical human data, they inadvertently inherit and amplify societal prejudices. For instance, biased facial recognition software and flawed predictive policing algorithms have been shown to disproportionately disadvantage minority communities. Moreover, the insatiable hunger of modern AI for training data has created a surveillance economy where personal privacy is constantly compromised. Massive corporations and governments now possess the ability to predict, manipulate, and control human behavior on a massive scale, threatening the foundational principles of democracy and individual autonomy.
Beyond these immediate societal impacts lies a deeper philosophical concern regarding the future of human creativity and critical thinking. As generative AI models become capable of writing essays, composing music, and creating stunning visual art, the line between human expression and machine output becomes increasingly blurred. If we rely too heavily on machines to generate our ideas and articulate our thoughts, we risk outsourcing the very cognitive processes that define our cultural and intellectual evolution.

This technological revolution offers unprecedented opportunities to solve some of humanity’s most complex challenges, but it also forces us to confront deep ethical dilemmas and existential questions about what it means to be human.
At the forefront of the AI revolution is its remarkable potential to enhance human capability and productivity. In the field of healthcare, machine learning algorithms are analyzing vast datasets of medical imaging and genetic sequences with a speed and accuracy that surpass human capabilities. This has led to the early detection of life-threatening diseases like cancer and the rapid development of novel pharmaceuticals, effectively saving countless lives. Similarly, in environmental science, AI systems are being deployed to model climate change patterns, optimize renewable energy grids, and track deforestation in real-time. The workplace of the future will likely not be one where humans are replaced by AI, but rather one where humans who use AI replace those who do not.

Because AI systems learn from historical human data, they inadvertently inherit and amplify societal prejudices. For instance, biased facial recognition software and flawed predictive policing algorithms have been shown to disproportionately disadvantage minority communities. Moreover, the insatiable hunger of modern AI for training data has created a surveillance economy where personal privacy is constantly compromised. Massive corporations and governments now possess the ability to predict, manipulate, and control human behavior on a massive scale, threatening the foundational principles of democracy and individual autonomy.
Beyond these immediate societal impacts lies a deeper philosophical concern regarding the future of human creativity and critical thinking. As generative AI models become capable of writing essays, composing music, and creating stunning visual art, the line between human expression and machine output becomes increasingly blurred. If we rely too heavily on machines to generate our ideas and articulate our thoughts, we risk outsourcing the very cognitive processes that define our cultural and intellectual evolution.

This has led to the early detection of life-threatening diseases like cancer and the rapid development of novel pharmaceuticals, effectively saving countless lives. Similarly, in environmental science, AI systems are being deployed to model climate change patterns, optimize renewable energy grids, and track deforestation in real-time. By processing variables too complex for the human mind to grasp simultaneously, AI acts as a cognitive amplifier, enabling scientists and policymakers to make data-driven decisions to protect our planet.
Furthermore, AI is fundamentally restructuring the global economy and the nature of work. Automation and intelligent systems have streamlined manufacturing pipelines, optimized supply chains, and revolutionized customer service through sophisticated natural language processing. While critics traditionally feared that automation would lead to widespread unemployment, historical trends suggest a more nuanced reality: a shift in the labor paradigm. While routine, repetitive tasks are increasingly handled by machines, new industries are emerging, creating a high demand for roles centered around AI ethics, data engineering, and human-machine collaboration. The workplace of the future will likely not be one where humans are replaced by AI, but rather one where humans who use AI replace those who do not.
However, this rapid integration of technology is not without its dark side. The rise of AI brings forth pressing ethical concerns, chief among them being algorithmic bias and the erosion of privacy. Because AI systems learn from historical human data, they inadvertently inherit and amplify societal prejudices. For instance, biased facial recognition software and flawed predictive policing algorithms have been shown to disproportionately disadvantage minority communities. Moreover, the insatiable hunger of modern AI for training data has created a surveillance economy where personal privacy is constantly compromised. Massive corporations and governments now possess the ability to predict, manipulate, and control human behavior on a massive scale, threatening the foundational principles of democracy and individual autonomy.
Beyond these immediate societal impacts lies a deeper philosophical concern regarding the future of human creativity and critical thinking. As generative AI models become capable of writing essays, composing music, and creating stunning visual art, the line between human expression and machine output becomes increasingly blurred. If we rely too heavily on machines to generate our ideas and articulate our thoughts, we risk outsourcing the very cognitive processes that define our cultural and intellectual evolution.

Founders & CEOs — We will place an AI-trained executive assistant inside your business, and if we don't place someone you want to hire… YOU DON'T PAY.

Keep reading below and I'll tell you:

#1 — How this works
#2 — Why we can make an offer this bold

/// How It Works ///

I own a company called Inside Out. We place AI-trained executive assistants with founders, CEOs, and operators.

Unlike every recruiter you've dealt with, we don't disappear after the hire.

We do four things:

We recruit them. Over 50,000 candidates screened every month, across the world. You only ever meet the finalists we already interviewed for you.

We train them. Every EA graduates our AI Academy before day one — so they run AI across your inbox, calendar, and admin and get through the work of several people. They also build SOPs documenting their entire role, so everything they do becomes a written system your business keeps forever.

We onboard them. It starts with our Executive Alignment Interview™, where your EA learns exactly how you work before touching anything: how you communicate, how you run your calendar, your pet peeves, your non-negotiables, what they can decide without you. Then a custom 90-day plan puts it into action — producing in week one, not quarter one.

We manage them. Daily check-ins through Cadence AI, our own performance management software, plus a dedicated success manager from our team.

/// Why We Can Promise This ///

We've helped over 1,500 businesses hire.

After that many placements, you learn exactly what separates the hires that stick from the ones that fall apart.

And it's almost never the recruiting. It's everything after.

Nobody trains them. Nobody onboards them properly. Nobody manages them.

That's why we structured the offer this way — we own all four stages, because that's what it actually takes for a hire to succeed.

/// The Terms ///

One-time placement fee. No monthly markups. No staffing-agency games.

If we don't find someone you want to hire → you don't pay it.

If it's ever not the right fit → free replacement.

The risk of the hire failing is on us, not you.

So if you're a founder, CEO, or operator running a real business and you're done doing $20/hour work…

Click this ad, watch the short video, and book a call.

— Chris

As a VA, have you ever had a client who says you're "invaluable"...

 who tells you they don't know how they’d run their business without you..

 ...but still pays you the same £25 an hour they started you on three years ago?

It's not that you're not skilled enough.

It's that nobody's ever taught you the difference between being relied on and being paid for it.

The truth is, being indispensable and being well paid are not the same thing. 

Nobody teaches you how to close that gap.

I know this one painfully well. 

I ended up doing VA work so I could do the school drop offs and be there for all the drop in sessions.

My first client paid me £444 a month and I was so proud of it.

But in every client relationship, I was doing more than I was ever paid for. 

Leading. Steering. Decision making.

Catching problems before they became problems. 

Nobody had a name for that. Including me.

Then AI started doing the parts of VA work that used to fill my week, the scheduling, the first drafts, the admin, in seconds. 

I watched it happen and I knew the ceiling wasn't going to move on its own.

Founders & CEOs — We will place an AI-trained executive assistant inside your business, and if we don't place someone you want to hire… YOU DON'T PAY.

Keep reading below and I'll tell you:

#1 — How this works
#2 — Why we can make an offer this bold

/// How It Works ///

I own a company called Inside Out. We place AI-trained executive assistants with founders, CEOs, and operators.

Unlike every recruiter you've dealt with, we don't disappear after the hire.

We do four things:

We recruit them. Over 50,000 candidates screened every month, across the world. You only ever meet the finalists we already interviewed for you.

We train them. Every EA graduates our AI Academy before day one — so they run AI across your inbox, calendar, and admin and get through the work of several people. They also build SOPs documenting their entire role, so everything they do becomes a written system your business keeps forever.

We onboard them. It starts with our Executive Alignment Interview™, where your EA learns exactly how you work before touching anything: how you communicate, how you run your calendar, your pet peeves, your non-negotiables, what they can decide without you. Then a custom 90-day plan puts it into action — producing in week one, not quarter one.

We manage them. Daily check-ins through Cadence AI, our own performance management software, plus a dedicated success manager from our team.

/// Why We Can Promise This ///

We've helped over 1,500 businesses hire.

After that many placements, you learn exactly what separates the hires that stick from the ones that fall apart.

And it's almost never the recruiting. It's everything after.

Nobody trains them. Nobody onboards them properly. Nobody manages them.

That's why we structured the offer this way — we own all four stages, because that's what it actually takes for a hire to succeed.

/// The Terms ///

One-time placement fee. No monthly markups. No staffing-agency games.

If we don't find someone you want to hire → you don't pay it.

If it's ever not the right fit → free replacement.

The risk of the hire failing is on us, not you.

So if you're a founder, CEO, or operator running a real business and you're done doing $20/hour work…

Click this ad, watch the short video, and book a call.

— Chris

body_text:
AI video might be the biggest unfair advantage creators have in 2026.

Because right now, attention is becoming harder to get — while AI is making attention-grabbing content easier to create.

Think about it.

Better products? Copied in weeks.
Better ads? Copied in days.
Better offers? Competitors can reverse-engineer them overnight.

But the audience you build while everyone else is still figuring this out?

**That’s yours.**

And right now, there’s a window.

AI lets one person with a laptop create realistic UGC, cinematic videos, AI influencers and scroll-stopping ads that used to require cameras, actors, editors and production teams.

Most people are still consuming this content.

The opportunity is learning how to **create it.**

Because attention compounds.

More content → more attention.
More attention → more opportunities.

cards.body:
Je me souviens la première fois que j'ai vu ce Bootcamp Microbiome...

J'étais en train de "scroller" sur mon téléphone, quand c'est apparu : ... "Résultats Garantis." Rien que ça, ça a capté mon attention, mais je suis passée à autre chose.

Pourquoi? 

Parce que ça ressemblait à toutes les autres promesses que j’avais déjà entendues.

J’ai essayé tellement de régimes, de programmes, de solutions miracles. 

Et je suis sûre que toi aussi, tu as vécu la même chose. Tu commences pleine de bonne volonté, tu te dis que cette fois, ça va marcher... 

Mais au bout de quelques jours, c’est la même histoire : la frustration, le manque d'énergie, la culpabilité de ne pas pouvoir suivre les règles à la lettre.

J’étais à ce stade-là. 

Je ne voulais plus de ces montagnes russes émotionnelles.

Mais cette fois-ci, quelque chose a piqué ma curiosité.

En parcourant les détails du programme, j’ai vu qu'il parlait de Microbiote Intestinal. 

Je me suis dit, tiens, c’est nouveau ça !

Je savais vaguement ce que c’était, mais je n’avais jamais fait le lien avec la perte de poids. Pourtant, ça faisait sens. 

Après tout, notre intestin influence tellement de choses dans notre corps.

Je suis allée me renseigner. J'ai lu des articles sur le microbiote, j'ai découvert comment il pouvait bloquer notre métabolisme, perturber notre digestion et même influencer notre humeur. 

J'ai appris que si ce petit écosystème dans nos intestins est déséquilibré, perdre du poids peut devenir presque impossible, même si on fait tout bien.

Là, j’ai commencé à réfléchir différemment.

Et si je n’étais pas le problème?

Et si ce que je devais vraiment faire, c’était d’arrêter de me battre contre mon propre corps et de commencer à en prendre soin?

Mais malgré ça, j’étais pas encore prête à sauter le pas. Parce que j’avais peur. 

Peur d’être déçue à nouveau, peur de ne pas tenir le coup, peur de refaire une énième tentative infructueuse.

Je continuais à penser à ce Bootcamp, à revenir sur la page, à me demander si ça pouvait vraiment fonctionner pour moi.

Pour être honnête, je détestais mon corps. Je manquais d’énergie, mon ventre était ballonné, et peu importe ce que je faisais, mon poids restait le même. J’étais à boute!

Un matin, après une nuit d'insomnie, je me suis levée en me disant «Go Mélanie! Je le fais!» 

Parce que j’en avais marre de ne rien faire et de détériorrer à vue d'oeil. Je me suis dit : «Pis si ça marche pas, il y a une garantie de remboursement, donc je perds rien!»

Mais imagine si ça marche? Je me trouverais stupide de pas l'essayer.

Donc je me suis inscrite.

Les premiers jours ont été surprenants. Ce n’était pas du tout ce à quoi je m’attendais. 

Pas de privation, pas de tapis roulant. 

Les recettes étaient délicieuses, je ne me suis JAMAIS sentie privée. Les vidéos étaient super motivantes, les techniques faciles, et ça me prenait seulement quelques minutes par jour, même pas!

Mais ce qui m’a le plus marqué, c’est à quel point je me suis sentie bien vite. Ma digestion s’est améliorée presque instantanément. Fini l'inflammation. Et pour la première fois depuis longtemps, je me suis réveillée avec plus d’énergie.

Au bout de 7 jours, non seulement j’avais perdu du poids, mais je me sentais surtout en meilleure forme que je ne l’avais été depuis 5 ans.

Et ça en 7 jours.

Ce Bootcamp-là m’a ouvert les yeux. 

En prenant soin de mon microbiote, en nourrissant mon corps avec les bons aliments et en suivant des conseils basés sur la science, j’ai vu des résultats que je n’avais jamais obtenus avec d’autres méthodes.

Aujourd’hui, je continue d’utiliser ce que j’ai appris dans le Bootcamp. 

Puisque j'ai mon accès à vie, chaque fois que je sens que mon énergie faiblit ou que je reprends du poids, je refais le programme. Et chaque fois, ça marche.

Je te partage tout ça parce que je sais ce que tu ressens en ce moment.

Je sais ce que c’est de voir une publicité et de se dire «Ça ne marchera pas pour moi.»

Mais crois-moi, si ce Bootcamp a pu m’aider, il peut t’aider aussi. 

Si tu es prête à enfin voir des résultats, si tu en as assez de te sentir épuisée, frustrée, et bloquée dans ton propre corps, je t’invite à faire ce que j’ai fait ce jour-là.

Inscris-toi. Tu n’as rien à perdre.

Pourquoi?

body_text:
Pickleball days means lots of movement, rallies, tawanan… and minsan, a little stumble along the way. 🏓💚 As a mom, gusto ko na ready kami for all the action. Kaya between rallies and after touching the ball, paddle, and court surfaces, quick sanitize muna before getting back in the game!
We always keep Green Cross Gentle Protect in our sports bag, ang gentlest sanitizer (with regular use) ng Green Cross na walang hapdi! (vs. other Green Cross alcohols and sanitizers. Based on clinical test.)
After that, game on ulit! ✨ And before we leave the court, may pahabol kaming #WalangHapdiMoves! 😂 We showed you ours, now it’s your turn! Try the #WalangHapdiMoves with your family and show us your moves!
#WalangHapdi #WalangHapdiWithXyza #GreenCrossGentleProtect
